title: A new study of former NFL players' brains found CTE in nearly 25%. What do experts say concerned current players should do about that?
description: The football ecosystem seems to tacitly acknowledge head injuries will not be eliminated from the sport anytime soon. Instead, the NFL, players union and researchers wonder how to treat the conditions that result from this inherent risk.
fullText:
A new study on the degeneration of NFL players' brains sent "a sobering reminder that football carries real risks," the NFL Players Association said Tuesday.

A study published in the British Medical Journal reported that at least 24.5% of former players' brains studied showed signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative condition diagnosed from X-rays showing abnormal protein clumps. As of now, the condition has been diagnosed only after death. The study analyzed the brains of former players who died between 2016 and 2021.

The union told its players in an email blast that the findings "should serve as a call to action across the entire football ecosystem." The NFL issued a statement that similarly preached proactive healthcare.

"The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust — and expanding — set of resources to enhance their physical and mental wellbeing," an NFL spokesperson said in a statement obtained by Yahoo Sports, in part. "We encourage former players to utilize these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health."

Identifying and seeking treatment during a former player's lifetime, some experts say, is an important step that research on postmortem diagnoses can overlook.

Dr. Rachel Grashow, the senior director of research initiatives for the Football Player Health Study at Harvard University, said the study's linkage between brain injury and CTE helps quantify the pathology, or study of the disease; but the scientific community and public definitions of CTE often don't align, Grashow said. People diagnosed with CTE have shown symptoms, including cognitive impairment, behavioral changes, mood changes and movement troubles, the Mayo Clinic says. But the postmortem diagnoses have complicated the ability to discern correlation from causation.

"As of yet, they haven't been able to tie symptoms," Grashow told Yahoo Sports by phone Tuesday night. "You can't connect symptoms to pathology yet."

What researchers believe they can do, and the NFL and NFLPA are emphasizing, is treat symptoms of repetitive brain injury during players' lives. The league, union and medical experts wonder whether healthcare adjustments during the years between a player's retirement and their death — a period often studied less than CTE research after their death — could reduce the severity of impact.

"Head injury causes a lot of conditions that aren't good for you," Grashow said. "But if you treat those conditions, that's possibly the best thing you can do for your brain, since you can't go in a time machine and undo how much head injury you had."

The NFL has tweaked rules in recent decades in hopes of reducing the frequency and severity of concussions and associated traumatic brain injuries.

Helmet regulations have advanced, including the increasing popularity of the league's Guardian Cap. Concussion protocols have become stricter and more formalized. The most dangerous phase of the game for head injuries — the NFL kickoff, where high-speed collisions unfolded often — has been overhauled.

Still, the football ecosystem seems to tacitly acknowledge head injuries will not be eliminated from the sport anytime soon. Instead, the league, union and researchers wonder how to treat the conditions that result from this inherent risk.

NFLPA executive director JC Tretter and NFLPA medical director Dr. Thom Mayer met with the lead author of the study published Tuesday, a union source told Yahoo Sports. Dr. Daniel Daneshvar of Massachusetts General Brigham and Boston University advised in an email to players: "Many of the symptoms associated with CTE are treatable with the right care."

"While we don't have a cure yet, we have seen improvements in players who receive care from doctors specializing in neurodegenerative disease and who know how to treat athletes," Daneshvar said, per the union email. "No one should walk away thinking there's nothing they can do."

The union will hold a call with medical experts in the coming weeks to answer player questions and create a forum for discussion, according to a copy of the union's email to players obtained by Yahoo Sports.

The league said it will continue to consider in-game safety strategies.

In the analysis of 5,000 living former players through Harvard's study, which receives funding from the NFLPA, Grashow and her colleagues have identified several elevated health risks for players.

Head injuries can cause high blood pressure, sleep apnea, low testosterone and depression, Grashow said. Oftentimes, players are living their post-career lives without treating those conditions, she said.

"It's so frustrating because it's like, we don't know what would happen if we actually treated the things that head injury caused," Grashow said. "We could see a totally different trajectory for these guys, but we haven't been doing that because I think there's such a tight coupling between the symptoms and the pathology and the hopelessness."

The league, players association and researchers overlap in their message to players about seeking healthcare as soon as symptoms arise, if not sooner.

In its Tuesday email entitled "New CTE Research: What Players Should Know," the union linked to more than half a dozen resources, including a checklist that players can bring to doctor's appointments to ensure professionals are heeding the most common conditions that have been found in current and former players.

From blood sugar and cholesterol to cognitive and emotional instability, the checklist aims to reduce players' need to research where they're most at risk.

"Playing football puts players at risk for a number of conditions that, if untreated, will absolutely hurt their brains over time," Grashow said. "The good news is that a lot of what it does impact can be tested for, often treated and managed."

Research of former players' brains often receives the most attention due to the fear and uncertainty surrounding degenerative brain conditions. But research of former players' bodies have shown more mixed results, including some encouraging signs.

A 2018 study of 9,778 former NFL players who played at least one season between 1986 and 2012 found that former players' mortality rates compared favorably to that of the general American male population. Former NFL players died at 46% the rate of U.S. men of the same age, race and calendar year, per the study published by the American College of Sports Medicine.

Former players in the study died at 65% the rate of their equivalent U.S. population from cardiovascular disease, the study found, a gap that widens far more for players with a body mass index that did not catapult them into the category of obesity. (Former players with Class 2 obesity or higher suffered from 2.2 times the cardiovascular disease-related deaths than the equivalent U.S. population.)

None of this erases the realities of research on players' brains, nor is it likely to assuage concerns of players and families. But researchers caution against fear and hype that can further trigger players' emotional unraveling or trust in medical professionals.

"I don't want to give people false hopes that treating these conditions are going to undo all the effects of football," Grashow said. "But if we know that players are living with these conditions and not getting them treated, having cognitive symptoms, likely due in some part to those conditions and then getting scared that they have CTE and leading to suicidality, then I think we've missed an opportunity at least to try to address some of those conditions."

Conversations around suicidal ideation have heightened during the last year after Cowboys defensive end Marshawn Kneeland and Minnesota Vikings receiver Rondale Moore died by suicide last November and February, respectively. Kneeland's family donated his brain to Boston University's CTE Center, which found Stage 1 CTE evidence in the 24-year-old's brain. (CTE is diagnosed by severity from Stage 1 through Stage 4.) Documented concerns about Kneeland's mental health had dated back to at least college, per records obtained by ESPN, and the Concussion and CTE Foundation emphasized that the diagnosis "should not be considered the cause of a suicide and is not known to be a risk factor for suicide."

Still, foundation CEO Dr. Chris Nowinski noted that Kneeland's CTE diagnosis came amid the league's current era of helmet and safety advancements.

"We have no reason to believe the current generation is at a lower risk of CTE than previous generations," Nowinski said in a statement. "Concussion protocols do not prevent CTE, because CTE is caused by repeated head impacts, not just concussions. If we want to reduce CTE risk, we must implement CTE prevention protocols and aggressively reduce the number and strength of head impacts at every level of the game."

Conversations with NFL decision-makers did not indicate the latest CTE research will spur any imminent rule or policy changes on the field. More research and awareness about proactive health measures during players' lives appear to be a stronger focus.

There will be some who wonder how well data from a brain bank, donated by families of players who often had symptoms that prompted concern, represents the non-donating player population. Others will look at this 24.5% finding as more measured than a previous CTE Center study that found CTE in 99% (110 of 111) brains donated to the bank. Daneshvar was also an author on that study, which some believe was skewed.

The authors of the latest study wrote in their finding that they hope this data analysis can "prove targets for future research studies and policy recommendations." The study's findings on the correlation between dementia and Stage 4 CTE at death could be among the topics on which researchers continue to seek clarity. Union warnings will continue to ring clear, too.

"Pay attention to your cognitive, neurological, and overall health," the NFLPA wrote in its email to players. "If you have concerns, seek evaluation and support. Early intervention matters. Resources are available today that can help."

description: Sean McVay and the Los Angeles Rams saw their first player fine of the 2026 campaign, thanks to rookie Darryl Peterson. The post NFL Delivers Punishment for Rams Rookie Outside Linebacker appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
Linebacker Darryl Peterson III is the first Los Angeles Rams player to receive punishment from the NFL this season.

Peterson and the Rams are preparing for their preseason finale against the Los Angeles Chargers, but the rookie undrafted free agent received notice over the past weekend about an infraction he committed in the opener against the Kansas City Chiefs.

It was a different kind of "welcome to the league" moment for Peterson.

In the aftermath, Peterson was fined $4,935 for his infraction, per the NFL's accountability hub.

Peterson is on a three-year, $3.1 million contract. The fine is a fraction of his $885,000 base salary and what the league could have charged him.

Per the league, horse collar infractions can cost as much as $17,911 for first-time offenses, and as much as $23,882 for a second. The fine levied against Peterson is 25.7% of the listed amount for a first-timer.

GettyChiefs LB Nick Bolton was fined for a horse-collar tackle on 49ers QB Brock Purdy in the Super Bowl.

The NFL makes itself clear to the Rams and every other team on most of its rules, particularly when it comes to regulating on-field player conduct. The penalty against Peterson is no exception to that.

"No player shall grab the inside collar of the back or the side of the shoulder pads or jersey, or grab the jersey at the name plate or above, and pull the runner toward the ground," the NFL's rulebook states. "This does not apply to a runner who is in the pocket area or in the area defined by close-line play. If his knees are buckled by the action, it is a foul, even if the runner is not pulled completely to the ground.

The penalty for a horse-collar tackle is, of course, a "loss of 15 yards and an automatic first down."

Otherwise, this was largely a learning experience for Peterson in Year 1 with the Rams. LA will close out the preseason on Thursday, August 27.

GettyRams DC Chris Shula has gotten a good look at Darryl Peterson III during the preseason.

Peterson has been racking up the snaps for head coach Sean McVay, defensive coordinator Chris Shula, and the Rams during the 2026 preseason slate. He played in Weeks 1 and 2.

Peterson has logged 4 total tackles in 69 snaps, per Pro Football Focus.

He is part of an edge rusher group led by reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett and 2025 Pro Bowler Byron Young. The Rams also lost Keir Thomas to an injury and replaced him on the roster with rookie UDFA Devean Deal.

LA still has DesJuan Johnson, Josaiah Stewart, and Tomon Fox, and another rookie UDFA in Wesley Bailey. Bailey stood out in Preseason Week 2 against the New Orleans Saints.

Peterson is very much still fighting for a spot on the Rams' 53-man roster.

title: Chiefs complete NFL trade with Giants to add help for Patrick Mahomes, Travis Kelce
description: The Kansas City Chiefs acquired OL Josh Ezeudu from the New York Giants for a 2028 seventh-round pick before their final preseason game. The Chiefs have had a very real concern about their offensive line all preseason, with a severe lack of depth behind their lead options, Kingsley Suamataia and Trey Smith.
fullText:
The Kansas City Chiefs acquired OL Josh Ezeudu from the New York Giants for a 2028 seventh-round pick before their final preseason game.

The Chiefs have had a very real concern about their offensive line all preseason, with a severe lack of depth behind their lead options, Kingsley Suamataia and Trey Smith.

With the offensive line playing an integral role in the success of the quarterback, the Chiefs have added reinforcements to their shallow o-line for Patrick Mahomes' protection.

ESPN reported the Chiefs' acquisition of Josh Ezeudu from the Giants to bolster their offensive line for a low cost.

Ezeudu is a 26-year-old former third-round pick who has appeared in 33 NFL games over his career. He's made only 10 starts and missed the entirety of last season with a calf injury.

Ezeudu can play as both a left and right guard, and has played at left tackle as well, showing he has the varied skill set a backup needs to fill in wherever required on the o-line.

That versatility can also give the Chiefs the room they need to develop a young option like Kahlil Benson in his preferred role rather than making him learn new styles on the fly as a floating backup.

The Chiefs' potential five-man offensive line of LT Josh Simmons, LG Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Smith, and RT Jaylon Moore can be elite, but they need to have strong backup options like Ezeudu to step up when required.

Their current backup options have been underwhelming throughout camp, so Ezeudu is a low-cost, high-upside swing for them.

Even a bad version of him would fit as a backup OL member, but even above-average production could make him a key backup.

The Chiefs need extra protection for Mahomes this season, especially early in the season, as he has to get comfortable after returning from a torn ACL.

This will in turn affect the kind of service options like Travis Kelce receive in what might be a retirement season for him.

Ezeudu has the talent and the size; it's just a question of him staying healthy enough to build momentum over the season and showcase his full strengths. If he does that, the Chiefs will be much better than anticipated.

title: Brain disease in dead NFL players 'higher than previously shown'
description: A new study says at least one in four ex-NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had a degenerative brain disease but the true figure could be much higher.
fullText:
As many as 97.7% of NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 could have had brain disease related to repeated blows to the head, a new study says.

Researchers looked at 878 former players who died during that period, with 235 having donated their brains to research.

Of those, 215 were found to have chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease which can only be diagnosed after death.

The study, published in the British Medical Journal, external, also found dementia was common among brain donors.

"We and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population," said the report's lead author Daniel Daneshvar, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School.

"These findings indicate that NFL players have a higher prevalence of CTE at death than has been previously shown in multiple community based studies."

Researchers calculated a "conservative minimum" of CTE prevalence among those who died in the six-year period to be 24.5% - rising to a "maximum" 97.7%.

They have urged the NFL to take prevention measures to reduce repetitive head impacts across all levels of the sport.

NFL admits football-brain disease link

New research finds link between head impacts & CTE

"The bulk of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn't occur at the NFL level," Danshvar said.

"They occurred at the collegiate level and at the high school level and in many cases the youth level. And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk."

An NFL spokesperson said: "The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.

"The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust - and expanding - set of resources to enhance their physical and mental well being.

"We encourage former players to utilise these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health."

CTE among American football players has been a growing issue in recent years. A 2011 Collective Bargaining Agreement for the NFL limited the number of contact practices.

Following a long-running class action, in 2016 the NFL agreed a $1bn (£700m) settlement with more than 5,000 former players.

title: Steelers Get Harsh Assessment From NFL Insider 3 Weeks Before Regular Season
description: An NFL insider is a little worried about the Pittsburgh Steelers this season after visiting them during a training camp tour. The post Steelers Get Harsh Assessment From NFL Insider 3 Weeks Before Regular Season appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The Pittsburgh Steelers are less than three weeks away from opening the regular season at Acrisure Stadium against the Atlanta Falcons. But they might not be heading toward winning back-to-back AFC North titles.

Sports Illustrated NFL Insider Albert Breer toured a handful of training camps this summer, and he told Fox Sports radio host Colin Cowherd that the Steelers could unravel fast this season.

"I think the obvious one might be Pittsburgh because of the age and the roster, Breer said Monday on "The Herd." "The construction of the team makes a lot of sense. If you think about it, it's Aaron Rodgers, and at receiver you got [Michael] Pittman Jr. and [DK] Metcalf, and you got Rico Dowdle coming in at running back and Pat Freiermuth at tight end. On defense, it's like veterans at every level. Cameron Heyward, T.J. Watt up front, Patrick Queen at linebacker, Jalen Ramsey, DeShon Elliott, and Jamel Dean in the secondary, and they have complex schemes coming in.

"Mike McCarthy is going to want to do a lot; he's going to be able to leverage a lot out of Aaron Rodgers becuase he's got veteran teammates. On defense, you've got Patrick Graham from the New England tree there going to try to throw a lot of volume at other offenses, and he's got the group to do it. It's just when you have that amount of age on your roster, you're walking a narrow path. Will the team wear down over the course of the year? What will practice look like in October and November, and will there be any injuries?"

It's no secret that the Steelers have the oldest roster in the NFL on average. According to Bill Speros at Bookies.com, the Steelers' roster averages 27 years and 98 days, about 96 days older than the next-oldest team, the Los Angeles Rams.

Having the oldest roster isn't the worst thing since a lot of veterans can help win games early on. But again, can the veterans stay healthy throughout a full season?

The Steelers might not have enough of a blend of youth and veterans to get through a full season and compete well into the playoffs.

Even though Breer might not be high on the Steelers this season, he liked what he saw from one of Pittsburgh's biggest rivals, the Cleveland Browns, this summer.

"The other one [training camp] where the energy sort of surprised me a little bit, and I guess it's timely considering everything that happened today was Cleveland," Breer added. "If you want to talk about being caught off guard a little bit, I just sensed really good energy with the Browns, and again, that is despite everything that's happened the last three or four days. But it does feel like Todd Monken has been able to inject a different feel to this team."

The Browns did seem to have good energy around them until they named Deshaun Watson the starting quarterback on Monday. Now it feels like Cleveland might not be on track to have a great season at all.

Pittsburgh should have a good chance of beating the Browns twice this season, and the first matchup between the two teams will be on "Thursday Night Football" in Cleveland in Week 4.

fullText:
Jets' 53-man roster prediction for 2026 NFL season appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

The New York Jets actually look like they have some genuine momentum. After dropping their preseason opener to Tampa Bay, Aaron Glenn's team responded with a statement performance in Pittsburgh. Suddenly, the competition for roster spots feels considerably more consequential. Geno Smith has already demonstrated that the offense can operate efficiently under Frank Reich. There defense has generated pressure and turnovers. With one preseason game remaining against the Giants, the Jets must separate legitimate contributors from temporary summer standouts. This will determine which 53 players give them the best chance to compete when the games finally count.

The Jets sit at 1-1 through two preseason games. They recovered from a 24-16 home defeat against Tampa Bay with a dominant 17-0 shutout of Pittsburgh at Acrisure Stadium. The encouraging response has given Glenn's revamped squad some much-needed confidence. Smith was particularly impressive in his preseason debut. He completed all seven of his passes on a touchdown drive while operating Reich's offense with efficiency and rhythm. Meanwhile, the defense overwhelmed Pittsburgh with four sacks and two takeaways. That offered a glimpse of the aggressive identity Glenn wants to establish. The Giants now provide the final measuring stick before New York must finalize its 53-man roster.

Quarterback (2): Geno Smith, Cade Klubnik

Smith has the experience and accuracy to serve as the unquestioned starter. His early preseason performance reinforced why the Jets believe he can provide stability. Reich's system should allow Smith to operate from structure while taking advantage of his ability to make quick decisions. Klubnik earns the backup spot. He gives New York a developmental option with enough mobility to expand the offense when necessary. The Jets ultimately cannot afford to devote a third roster spot to the position.

Running Back (5): Breece Hall, Braelon Allen, Isaiah Davis, Kene Nwangwu, Andrew Beck

Hall remains the centerpiece because of his home-run potential. The Jets have every reason to maximize his touches. Allen provides physicality and complementary early-down work. Davis gives the team another capable runner. Nwangwu's value extends beyond the backfield because of his special-teams ability. Beck's fullback versatility makes him particularly useful in short-yardage packages. It is an unusually deep group, but every member offers a distinct role.

Wide Receiver (6): Garrett Wilson, Adonai Mitchell, Omar Cooper Jr, Tim Patrick, Arian Smith, Isaiah Williams

Wilson should remain the primary target in Reich's passing attack. His ability to win at multiple levels gives Smith a reliable option. Mitchell brings size and vertical ability. Patrick supplies veteran experience and contested-catch reliability. Cooper and Arian Smith add explosiveness. Williams provides versatility from multiple alignments.

Tight End (3): Mason Taylor, Kenyon Sadiq, Jelani Woods

Taylor projects as an important receiving component. Sadiq adds athleticism and the ability to threaten defenses vertically. Woods provides a massive target and a useful option in the red zone.

Offensive Line (9): Olu Fashanu, Dylan Parham, Josh Myers, Joe Tippmann, Armand Membou, Max Mitchell, Chukwuma Okorafor, Xavier Newman, Anez Cooper

Fashanu anchors the left side. Membou handles the right tackle position. Myers gives the interior a veteran presence at center. Parham and Tippmann complete the projected starting configuration. The depth is arguably just as important. Mitchell's ability to play multiple positions, Okorafor's tackle experience, and Newman's interior versatility provide insurance against potential injuries.

Defensive line (5): T'Vondre Sweat, Harrison Phillips, David Onyemata, Jowon Briggs, Darrell Jackson Jr

Sweat and Phillips provide substantial size and power. Onyemata adds veteran savvy and pass-rushing experience. Briggs offers rotational flexibility, with Jackson providing additional depth. The objective is clear: force opposing offenses to account for the interior before they can attack the Jets' edge rushers.

EDGE (5): David Bailey, Will McDonald IV, Joseph Ossai, Kingsley Enagbare, Nate Lynn

McDonald is the explosive pass-rushing threat capable of changing games. Bailey and Ossai provide additional pressure packages. Enagbare brings versatility and experience, and Lynn rounds out the rotation.

Linebacker (4): Demario Davis, Jamien Sherwood, Francisco "Kiko" Mauigoa, Marcelino McCrary-Ball

Davis supplies the veteran leadership and football intelligence. Sherwood complements him with athleticism and range. Mauigoa and McCrary-Ball provide younger rotational options. The Jets do not need this group to dominate statistically if the defensive line and secondary can consistently create favorable situations.

Cornerback (6): Brandon Stephens, Nahshon Wright, Jarvis Brownlee Jr, Azareye'h Thomas, D'Angelo Ponds, Qwan'tez Stiggers

Stephens provides experience on the perimeter. Wright adds another lengthy coverage option. Brownlee and Thomas give the Jets additional physicality. Ponds and Stiggers provide depth and developmental upside.

Safety (5): Minkah Fitzpatrick, Andre Cisco, Dane Belton, Malachi Moore, Samuel Womack III

Fitzpatrick gives Glenn the freedom to move him around the formation. Cisco brings playmaking ability. Belton, Moore, and Womack provide rotational and special-teams value.

Kicker: Jason Sanders
Punter: Austin McNamara
Long Snapper: Thomas Hennessy.

Sanders gives the Jets a proven option at kicker. McNamara handles punting and holding duties. Hennessy provides continuity at long snapper. With the rest of the roster undergoing significant transition, maintaining stability here is particularly valuable.

The Jets' projected roster reflects a team attempting to establish a completely different identity. Smith and Hall provide recognizable offensive pillars. Wilson gives the passing game a legitimate focal point. The combination of Fitzpatrick, Davis, and an aggressive front gives Glenn the ingredients for a physical defense.

The biggest question is whether the depth chart can translate the optimism of August into sustained regular-season performance. For a Jets organization attempting to turn encouraging flashes into meaningful progress, the final 53-man roster may be the first real blueprint of what this new era intends to become.

description: Are the Minnesota Vikings already taking calls for J.J. McCarthy?

title: Mike Vrabel reveals why he doesn't play Drake Maye in NFL Preseason
description: Drake Maye had a breakout "sophomore" NFL season. His head coach, Mike Vrabel, elaborated on the decision not to play Maye this preseason.
fullText:
In his first full season as an NFL starting quarterback, Drake Maye quickly proved himself as the New England Patriots' next franchise quarterback.

Maye finished his sophomore season with 4,394 passing yards, 31 passing touchdowns and a 77.1 QBR, finishing Top-4 in each category. Add 450 rushing yards and four more scores, Maye helped New England clinch its first AFC East title since the 2019-20 NFL season. 1,000 postseason scrimmage yards and seven touchdowns later, Maye put the Pats back in their first Super Bowl – also since 2019.

As is customary with established starters, Maye isn't playing in the preseason, sitting out both of New England's first two games. During a Monday appearance on Massachusetts-based radio station WEEI, head coach Mike Vrabel elaborated on his decision to not play Patriots starters.

"We are the front office," Vrabel said via ESPN's Mike Reiss. "We are all making the decisions. We're all included in this. It was about the young guys we have to develop. You can see that the players we kept out of the game, those are the guys. And we have to be able to find some guys behind them to be backups, to be the first guy in … those are the things that we are trying to develop and I guess that's what I was referencing."

Don't expect to see Maye during New England's preseason finale this coming Thursday, which will be an 8 p.m. kickoff at the 0-2 Cleveland Browns.

When the Patriots open their regular season with a Super Bowl rematch at the Seattle Seahawks, expect Maye to continue as a featured part of the reigning AFC East Champions' offense.

title: NFL legend Ray Lewis brings more than photo op to Community School of Naples
description: NFL legend Ray Lewis visited Community School of Naples, speaking to high school and Pop Warner players about mental health for young athletes.
fullText:
Ray Lewis didn't know how to slow down.

He was wearing half pads, and his high school football coach had made it clear: There would be no tackling.

Then the play happened. Lewis hit the player anyway.

His coach couldn't believe it. He had just told the players there would be no tackling.

Lewis' response: "Coach, that wasn't even full speed."

"Don't change it. We'll change around you."

Decades later, that mentality still defines Lewis. It followed him from Lakeland Kathleen High School to the University of Miami and through 17 NFL seasons in Baltimore.

But the lesson Lewis took from that moment wasn't simply about playing hard. It was about having a coach who understood him.

Now, Lewis is trying to provide that same kind of influence for a new generation.

The Pro Football Hall of Famer spent part of Saturday, Aug. 22, at the Community School of Naples, talking with coaches, players and teachers before later addressing a smaller audience on campus during a Fellowship of Christian Athletes event.

"I'd do this the rest of my life for free," Lewis told USA TODAY Sports. "I want to see a young man that says, 'I get it.' A few of these kids came to me later (today) and said, 'I'm really struggling.' And they will never tell nobody else that. But you expose who you are. That's why I always give them my weaknesses. If you know my weaknesses, then you can appreciate my strengths.

"But if you don't know where I came from, then you're just gonna look at me as, 'Oh my gosh, you're Ray Lewis.' A lot comes with that. That's why I come to schools like this; it's a bonus. It's what I live my life with. Making the transition of losing my child, every time I take one of these boys' hands, I'm blessing somebody else."

Lewis shared plenty of stories about his past. His mother was 15 when she had him. He grew up without his biological father and watched his mother struggle to provide for him and his siblings.

Football wasn't initially an option because his family couldn't afford the $15 required to play. He went to practices anyway, sitting outside the gate and crying because he couldn't join the other players.

Then, in 1985, a coach approached him and asked why he wasn't playing. Lewis told him.

The coach went to his mother. After a three-hour conversation, Lewis got his chance.

That coach became one of the people Lewis still credits with changing his life. So did the coaches who followed.

Every coach Lewis had from high school and college remains in his phone. He still talks to them and sends them annual Father's Day messages. Three of them attended his Hall of Fame ceremony.

He didn't just listen to those coaches. He absorbed them.

He asked questions about drills and technique, often using the car rides home to understand why his coaches directed him to do something a certain way.

Looking back, Lewis believes his childhood circumstances made him more willing to learn from those men.

"I recognized them (at my Hall of Fame) because they gave me the leadership that my father wasn't around to give me," Lewis said. "... Every one of my coaches gave me that. All leadership, all fatherhood, all discipline, all responsibility, all integrity, all the character."

That experience shaped the way Lewis thinks about coaching. It's also part of why he has become so focused on what happens to young people away from the football field.

Lewis has partnered with Baltimore County Public Schools on a program focused on students' mental and emotional well-being. Launched in March, the pilot mental health screening program is set to enter its first full school year in Baltimore, with hopes of expanding the initiative statewide.

The work has taken on added meaning for Lewis following the loss of his eldest son in 2023, and he often speaks to kids about the importance of not being afraid to be vulnerable.

"You check their 40 (time), you check their hips," Lewis said. "You'll check their surgery history. But you won't check their minds."

He talked at CSN about how difficult it is for many young people to open up, particularly in a world where social media can make perception feel more important than reality. When young people know somebody genuinely cares about them, they're often willing to say things they have been holding inside.

CSN football player Benjamin Reseau was one of them.

Hearing Lewis' story didn't feel like listening to a distant NFL legend recount Reseau's childhood. The Seahawks senior saw parts of his own life in it.

Lewis talked about growing up without his father. Reseau lost his father to coronavirus during the pandemic. Lewis talked about his relationship with his mother, who he has described as his best friend. Reseau shares the same sentiment.

"I saw a connection in a lot of his characteristics and a lot of the things he's done over his life," Reseau said.

That connection made Lewis' message more personal.

Reseau previously struggled to open up about his own experiences, in part because he was afraid of being judged. Coming to CSN, where many students had grown up in circumstances far different from his own, made it difficult at times to explain what he had been through.

Over time though, he learned that keeping things inside wasn't helping. So when Lewis spoke, Reseau listened.

"I just thought today, something just told me to speak up," Reseau said. "I had to."

Lewis made sure to talk to Reseau after the discussion, and the two exchanged phone numbers.

"No one I've coached has handled so much adversity with grace," CSN football coach Jonah Dubinski said of Reseau.

For Dubinski, that was part of the challenge Lewis was addressing.

"We have kids on both extremes socioeconomically and culturally, and how do you reach those different kinds of kids with the same message?" Dubinski said. "And Ray's advice there was fantastic. Get away from results-driven analysis of performance and be process- and structure-oriented.

"That's dead on. You listen to (Nick) Saban, you listen to Ray Lewis, you listen to everyone who's done it at a high level. It's process-oriented."

That philosophy extends beyond football for Dubinski. CSN's goal is to develop young men and women first, trusting that the results on the field will follow. That's part of why having Lewis in the building carried more weight than simply showing the players a video or playing a motivational speech.

"A lot of what he said today, you can piece together from the hundreds of videos out there," Dubinski said. "But it impacted me differently. It certainly impacted the kids differently."

Two parts of Lewis' message particularly stuck with Reseau: hearing Lewis talk about losing his son and hearing him discuss the relationships he has maintained with his coaches.

Reseau said he already tries to maintain those relationships with his own coaches beyond football.

"I always try to make sure I'm connected with everybody on another level, like a relationship type," Reseau said. "Always try to leave a good footprint for myself, for everybody."

Lewis left the players with another piece of advice:

"Stop asking for the picture," he said. "Ask for knowledge."

title: Former Penn State 1,000-Yard WR Labeled as NFL's Most Overpaid WR
description: Penn State has sent plenty of good players to the NFL over the years, with Saquon Barkley being one of the best. He earned a huge payday from the Philadelphia Eagles and is well worth his huge extension.
fullText:
Penn State has sent plenty of good players to the NFL over the years, with Saquon Barkley being one of the best. He earned a huge payday from the Philadelphia Eagles and is well worth his huge extension.

But not all of the former Nittany Lions players in the NFL are worth as much as they are getting paid right now. Some are earning more than they maybe should, considering their talents.

In Garrett Podell of CBS Sports' opinion, one former Penn State wide receiver, who had over 1,000 yards in one season with the Nittany Lions, is the most overpaid WR in the NFL. That WR is Tampa Bay Buccaneers veteran Chris Godwin.

"Chris Godwin's three-year, $66 million extension is aging like spoiled milk," Podell writes. "He has missed a combined 18 games over the last two seasons, eight of which came in 2025, when he registered career lows in catches (33) and receiving yards (360) while producing the second-fewest receiving touchdowns of his career (two)."

Godwin is a 30-year-old wide receiver who was drafted in the third round, at 84th overall, by the Buccaneers back in 2017.

He's since won a Super Bowl, catching passes from Tom Brady, and was named a Pro Bowler back in 2019 when he had 1,333 receiving yards.

In his NFL career, Godwin has 612 receptions on 867 targets for 7,626 yards and 41 touchdowns. He's also one first-down shy of 400 for his NFL career.

Godwin is one of the best WRs to come out of Penn State in school history, but now, at 30 years old entering his 10th season in the league, he's considered the most overpaid WR in the league.

Spending $22 million per-year on Godwin is a bit too much, considering he just had back-to-back seasons playing under 10 games and recording under 600 receiving yards.

During his time at Penn State, only his freshman season, when he caught 26 passes for 338 yards and two TDs, was worse. He had 1,101 yards and five TDS in 2015, and 982 yards and 11 TDs in 2016.

While Godwin could bounce back in 2026 for the Buccaneers, the former Penn State star WR is currently overpaid and is arguably the most overpaid WR in the NFL.

But even if he doesn't do a whole lot more for the rest of his NFL career, it's still been a massive success for the Nittany Lions WR in the NFL, as he's been arguably the best WR Penn State has ever sent to the league.

title: NFL predictions: Previewing all 16 AFC teams & predicting every record in 2026
description: Division winners, win totals, playoff teams, and more!
fullText:
The 2026 NFL season is almost here, and the AFC looks loaded from top to bottom. Every division has at least one legitimate contender, while several teams could make the jump from afterthought to playoff team. Here is my division-by-division breakdown and prediction for all 16 AFC teams.

MORE: 5 most improved NFL offenses entering 2026-2027 season

Dec 21, 2025; Cleveland, Ohio, USA; Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) warms up prior to a game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field. Mandatory Credit: Ken Blaze-Imagn Images

The Bills remain the safest bet in this division. Josh Allen is still the centerpiece, but the biggest change comes with Joe Brady taking over as head coach and Jim Leonhard running the defense. Buffalo also added DJ Moore to a receiving corps that desperately needed another difference-maker. The Bills won 12 games last season, and I expect them to remain near the top of the AFC. Prediction: 11-6, AFC East champions.

It's difficult to bet against the reigning AFC champions after what they accomplished last season. Drake Maye has another year of experience, and New England added A.J. Brown to an offense that already averaged 28.8 points per game in 2025. The Patriots will have enormous expectations, but I expect them to remain a serious contender. Prediction: 11-6, playoff team.

The Jets are better than the Dolphins, but that's not saying much. Geno Smith returns after leading the NFL in interceptions last season, while New York has completely reshaped its roster and enters 2026 with three first-round picks. There is enough talent here to surprise people, but the quarterback play has to improve dramatically. Prediction: 6-11.

Miami feels like a rebuilding team after moving on from Tua Tagovailoa and Tyreek Hill. Malik Willis now has an enormous opportunity, but expecting everything to click immediately is asking a lot. The Dolphins could be competitive in stretches, but this looks like the toughest roster in the division. Prediction: 5-12.

Dec 7, 2025; Baltimore, Maryland, USA; Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson (8) warms up before the game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Peter Casey-Imagn Images

The Ravens are my pick to bounce back after an ugly 8-9 season. John Harbaugh is gone, and Jesse Minter takes over, while Lamar Jackson gets a new offensive coordinator in Declan Doyle. Baltimore also added Trey Hendrickson and could get Nnamdi Madubuike back, potentially transforming a defense that struggled badly last year. Prediction: 11-6, AFC North champions.

Joe Burrow's health remains the biggest variable, but Cincinnati finally appears serious about fixing its defense. The Bengals added Jonathan Allen, Boye Mafe, Bryan Cook and Kyle Dugger before acquiring Dexter Lawrence. If Burrow stays healthy, this could be a dangerous team. Prediction: 10-7, playoff team.

The Steelers are fascinating because Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers could either make this look like a brilliant move or a desperate one. Pittsburgh also added Michael Pittman Jr., giving Rodgers another legitimate target. The defense has to improve, though, after ranking 26th in total defense last season. Prediction: 9-8.

The Browns are still rebuilding. Todd Monken takes over as head coach, the quarterback situation remains unsettled, and Cleveland traded Myles Garrett after his record-setting 2025 season. Jared Verse gives the defense a new centerpiece, but I don't expect the Browns to contend yet. Prediction: 5-12.

Division winner: Baltimore Ravens

MORE: 4 NFL players with most pressure entering 2026-2027 season

Houston Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud (7) throws during the first half of an AFC Wild Card Round game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium. Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images

The Texans are one of the most difficult teams to project. They went 12-5 last season and have an outstanding defense, but C.J. Stroud needs to rediscover his rookie form. Houston also completely revamped its offensive line and added David Montgomery to improve the running game. If the line finally stabilizes, the Texans could be a Super Bowl contender. Prediction: 11-6, AFC South champions.

Jacksonville won 13 games last season and remains one of the AFC's most intriguing teams. Travis Etienne is gone, leaving Bhayshul Tuten and others to replace his production, while Travis Hunter's two-way role will be fascinating to watch. If Brian Thomas Jr. takes a step forward, and Parker Washington continues his ascent, this offense could be dangerous. Prediction: 10-7, playoff team.

The Colts' entire season may depend on Daniel Jones staying healthy. Indianapolis saw its offense fall apart when Jones was injured last year, and the team is also dealing with major health questions involving Jonathan Taylor and DeForest Buckner. There's talent here, but too much uncertainty for me to trust them as a playoff team. Prediction: 8-9.

Everything revolves around Cam Ward. Tennessee brought in Robert Saleh and Brian Daboll to help develop its young quarterback and added veteran receiver Wan'Dale Robinson along with first-round pick Carnell Tate. I expect improvement, but the Titans are still a year away from seriously competing. Prediction: 6-11.

Division winner: Houston Texans

Jan 17, 2026; Denver, CO, USA; Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix (10) calls an audible during the first quarter of an AFC Divisional Round playoff game against the Buffalo Bills at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Denver is my pick to win the AFC West. The Broncos went 14-3 last season, largely kept their roster intact, and added Jaylen Waddle to give Bo Nix another elite weapon. The biggest question is Nix's health after his ankle injury, but if he's healthy, Denver has the most complete roster in the division. Prediction: 12-5, AFC West champions.

The Chiefs are coming off a stunning 6-11 season, so there's nowhere to go but up. Patrick Mahomes remains the ultimate reason for optimism, but Kansas City has more questions than we've seen in years. I expect a bounce-back season, just not another dominant run through the division. Prediction: 10-7, playoff team.

The Chargers should once again be competitive with Justin Herbert and Jim Harbaugh, but their offensive line health remains a concern. The addition of tight end David Njoku gives Herbert more options, and the defense should keep them in games. Still, I don't see them winning this division. Prediction: 9-8.

The Raiders may be the AFC's most intriguing long-term project. No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza is behind veteran Kirk Cousins for now, while Las Vegas also made significant offensive-line upgrades. If Cousins struggles, the pressure to unleash Mendoza will become enormous. Prediction: 6-11.

Division winner: Denver Broncos

Aug 15, 2026; Kansas City, Missouri, USA; Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes (15) on field against the Los Angeles Rams during the first half of the pre season game at Arrowhead Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

My AFC playoff field would be Buffalo, Baltimore, Houston and Denver as division winners, with New England and Cincinnati, and Kansas City earning wild-card spots.

The AFC should be extremely competitive, but I see Denver, Baltimore and Houston as the three teams best positioned to challenge Buffalo and New England for the conference crown. There are plenty of variables that could change the picture once the regular season begins, but on paper, the AFC looks like it could be an absolute battle from Week 1 through the playoffs.

title: ‘No Pity From Me,’ ‘Should’ve Booed Louder’ — Deshaun Watson Gets on NFL Fans’ Nerves After Divisive Remarks on Getting Booed at Home
description: Deshaun Watson’s comments after the Cleveland Browns’ 31-7 preseason loss to the Buffalo Bills have added another layer to the team’s ongoing quarterback drama. Watson was met with loud boos when he entered the game in the second half after Shedeur Sanders started the contest.
fullText:
Deshaun Watson's comments after the Cleveland Browns' 31-7 preseason loss to the Buffalo Bills have added another layer to the team's ongoing quarterback drama.

Watson was met with loud boos when he entered the game in the second half after Shedeur Sanders started the contest. Afterward, Watson called the reaction "disrespectful" and "personal," prompting an immediate response from NFL fans.

The boos rang out as soon as Watson's name was announced at the beginning of the second half. Speaking after the game, Watson said he believes the reaction went beyond his on-field performance.

"I think the whole world knows it has nothing to do about the performance," Watson said after Saturday's preseason action. "It's a little bit more personal than that. So, I think that's a disrespectful thing."

Watson also referenced his previous injury (from back in 2024) in Cleveland, adding, "Last time I played on this field, I tore my Achilles. That same fanbase, they cheered when I got hurt."

His comments quickly spread across social media, with fans largely pushing back against the quarterback's perspective.

Pranav Sriraman summed up his reaction bluntly: "Should've booed louder."

NFL analyst Max Loeb also suggested Watson's comments showed just how strained the relationship has become. "If you didn't think things were already too far gone in Cleveland with Deshaun Watson… Watch this clip."

Joey Knish questioned why Watson remains with the Browns at all: "Why the [expletive] is this guy even on the team? The Browns want to lose and draft a QB. The fanbase HATES Watson. There's a 0% chance anybody trades for him. Just send his [expletive] home."

Kev focused on what he viewed as Watson portraying himself as the victim. "This guy playing the victim card is wild for 100 reasons." A co-host at Fox Sports Radio even suggested the Browns should consider moving on immediately: "Send him to the NY Jets and get this [expletive] over with before it gets ugly."

Analyst Jared Monroe offered one of the harshest assessments of Watson's situation in Cleveland: "No pity from me. You can either be a bad person or bad at your job. You can't be both. Deshaun's wasted guaranteed bag set the Browns back more than a decade."

NFL writerBrian Drake was similarly critical, arguing that Watson's relationship with the fanbase may be beyond repair: "Browns owe Deshaun Watson $46M guaranteed. But it's over. The fans will never accept him after his scumbag actions. Make him inactive every week, then move on. He'll likely never play another down in the NFL."

The reaction comes as Cleveland continues to evaluate Watson and second-year quarterback Shedeur Sanders.

Sanders started the second preseason matchup and immediately provided a spark. He completed his first eight passes and capped Cleveland's opening drive with an 8-yard touchdown pass to Luke Floriea.

Watson struggled after taking over in the second half. He completed 5 of 12 passes for 36 yards and threw an interception as Cleveland's offense failed to find any rhythm.

With head coach Todd Monken yet to announce a Week 1 starter ahead of the Browns' opener against Jacksonville, the game against Buffalo only added to the debate.

For Cleveland, the decision now involves more than simply comparing two quarterbacks. Sanders has energized the fanbase, while Watson is facing increasing frustration from supporters who have already made their feelings clear.

The Browns will ultimately have to decide whether Watson's experience and contract situation outweigh Sanders' momentum and growing support in Cleveland.

title: Rams backups highlight the NFL's flawed beauty in 34-0 win over Saints
description: One play. A lifetime of waiting. Alex Cook's 100-yard interception return for a touchdown was a prayer whispered into existence. But in the cruel mathematics of NFL, one moment of glory might not be enough. Read the story of the Rams' 34-0 shutout and the men fighting for one more tomorrow.
fullText:
INGLEWOOD, Calif.––Thousands of football fans traveled through an asphalt skillet and sun-baking rays to sit in SoFi Stadium air thick with the smell of polyethylene pellets and concession food, littering empty seats and staring down at a field full of men fighting for their lives.

Peter Pan lost his shadow in Wendy Darling's nursery. Peter Pan never played football. Peter Pan never had to stare down the barrel of an NFL roster cut or feel the August sun bake his last hope into the turf.

Not the marquee names. The other ones.

The marquee names are set. The stars sleep in their beds while the backups, the special teamers and the practice-squad hopefuls run themselves into the ground for 60 minutes of tape that might buy them 60 more days in a uniform.

The ones who know the difference between making the 53-man roster and making a phone call home that changes everything.

For one afternoon in Inglewood, the Rams' backups played like they had nothing to lose and everything to prove.

The New Orleans Saints never stood a chance in the 34-0 drubbing.

For most of these men, the dream of regular-season action is not dying; it is already dead.

But on this Saturday in Inglewood, the dead refused to lie down.

Cam Lampkin has been the shadow of every receiver he covered.

Edwin So - The Sporting Tribune

Los Angeles Rams cornerback Cam Lampkin (21) daps up with teammates during an NFL preseason game between the New Orleans Saints and Los Angeles Rams on Saturday, August 22, 2026 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

At 5-foot-11 he is not the biggest name in the Rams secondary.

He is neither Trent McDuffie nor Jaylen Watson.

Lampkin is a name many overlook when they check the depth chart. But on Saturday, he made Zach Wilson feel like Captain Hook in the first half––searching, swiping, finding nothing but empty air and regret.

Wilson dropped back––looked left, looked right. Wilson found only the sticky fingers of coverage. The pass rush and coverage have a symbiotic relationship; one hand washes the other. Even without Myles Garrett, Kobie Turner, McDuffie or Watson playing, the New Orleans Saints stood no chance against Los Angeles' coverage unit.

Wilson completed just 6 of 12 passes for 55 yards in the first half and an abysmal 28.1 quarterback rating. The kind of number that gets a man cut before the team plane lands.

Lampkin played with coverage so sticky that Super Glue would envy. Every receiver he faced found a shadow that moved with them, anticipated their breaks and swallowed their hope.

"He did a great job," Sean McVay said. "You know, I thought we were in positions to understand a lot of the coverages."

Al'Zillion Hamilton jumped a hook route early in the second quarter. Wilson threw it right to him. It was the kind of play that separates guys who stick around from guys who don't. It was not merely an interception; it was an invitation accepted.

Edwin So - The Sporting Tribune

Los Angeles Rams quarterback Stetson Bennett IV (13) hands the ball off during an NFL preseason game between the New Orleans Saints and Los Angeles Rams on Saturday, August 22, 2026 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

Then Stetson Bennett took over.

He played like a man possessed, completing 19 of 31 passes for 181 yards and rushing for two touchdowns.

He scrambled when the pocket collapsed. He scrambled to make plays. He scrambled for his football life.

It started in the first quarter. Fourth and 1.

Bennett feathered a pass over double coverage to Tyler Scott, who laid out like a man diving for loose change on a sidewalk. Scott had an earlier ball bounce off his hand on a would-be touchdown, but this time, he held on.

"The flat guy got ran into," Bennett said. "I was just thinking put it in a safe spot so T Scott (Tyler Scott) can go get it."

The drive stalled in the red zone, and Harrison Mevis netted a 26-yard field goal to give the Rams backups a leap forward and a 3-0 score.

Bennet later scored on a 1-yard scramble after the refs deliberated and later ruled it a touchdown. Mevis nailed the PAT to extend the lead 10-0.

In the second quarter, with the Saints in man-to-man coverage and no one on the defense accounting for him, Bennett scrambled to the right when Saints edge rusher Garrett Nelson didn't keep containment.

Bennett looked like a gamer and orchestrated scoring drives throughout the game.

"It feels more comfortable out there than in years prior," Bennett said.

Edwin So - The Sporting Tribune

Los Angeles Rams defensive back Alex Cook (39) runs to the end zone for a touchdown during an NFL preseason game between the New Orleans Saints and Los Angeles Rams on Saturday, August 22, 2026 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

Alex Cook has not played in the NFL since 2023. He came from the UFL. He dreamed of being back. He dreamed of one more pick-six.

In the third quarter, Spencer Rattler drove the Saints down the field. The goal line loomed. The Rams' defense bent. Rattler threw to Treyton Welch on a hitch route.

Drove on the ball. Undercut the route. Caught it in stride.

Then he ran 100 yards for a pick-six that stretched the Rams' lead to 27-0 and sucked whatever life remained out of the Saints' sideline.

A lifetime of waiting collapsed into 15 seconds of glory.

"I was dreaming like, man, if I could just get one more pick six back in the NFL, that would make my whole life," Cook said. "Thank God I was able to get one today."

He finished with one tackle on defense and one on special teams. One hundred yards on one play. One tackle on every other play. The math of the NFL is cruel; the NFL's poetry––astonishing.

Cook's journey to this moment was anything but linear. He came from the UFL. He has fought, scratched and clawed his way back onto an NFL sideline. The Rams gave him a chance; he is not wasting it.

"We were in a typical cover four," Cook explained. "I knew that spot route was going to come sit right at the end zone and I was just waiting for the QB to throw."

When the throw came, Cook jumped it. He had inside leverage. He had position. He had the instincts of a player who has been doing this since he was a kid.

"I need some more oxygen," Cook joked. "I was beyond tired. But seriously, you just got to reset your mind. It's the next play mentality."

The sideline celebration told a different story. Teammates mobbed him. They recognized what the moment meant. For him. For his carrer. For his life.

"That was so cool," Cook said. "That just a testament of this team and the culture Sean McVay has built."

Edwin So - The Sporting Tribune

The New Orleans Saints fumble the ball near the end zone during an NFL preseason game between the New Orleans Saints and Los Angeles Rams on Saturday, August 22, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

Then Wesley Bailey, who lived in the backfield, forced a fumble. in the third quarter.

The Saints had driven deep into Rams territory. A touchdown would cut into the lead. Bailey punched the ball free from Ty Chandler, and Payton Zdroik recovered at the 2-yard line.

A red-zone turnover. A momentum killer. A difference.

Bailey finished with five tackles, a sack, three pressures, a tackle for loss, a forced fumble and four QB hits––a performance so complete that McVay couldn't stop talking about it.

"You felt his presence all day," McVay said. "There's certain guys you just kind of feel on defense where you just know they're making their presence felt."

"Being able to get a red zone turnover is great," Bailey said. "For him to come out with nothing is definitely great."

But the final score is not the story.

The story is what happens next week when the coaching staff gathers in a room and decides who gets to keep chasing their dream and who gets a handshake, a thank-you, and a phone number for their agent.

Sean McVay stood at the podium. His voice carried the weight of a man who has been on both sides of these cuts.

"I thought it was a really just good team effort," McVay said. "Awesome to see so many guys making plays."

He praised Bennett's command. He praised Bailey's presence. He praised the secondary.

"Repetition is the mother of learning," McVay said.

But repetition is also the father of heartbreak.

These players have repeated the drills. They have repeated the routes. They have repeated the dream. Soon, they will wait.

Edwin So - The Sporting Tribune

New Orleans Saints quarterback Spencer Rattler (2) makes a pass during an NFL preseason game between the New Orleans Saints and Los Angeles Rams on Saturday, August 22, 2026 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

The Los Angeles Rams' second preseason game was much more stress-free than the first.

Neither team played its starters. But the Rams' backups were clearly much better than New Orleans'. It is a compliment to the depth the Rams have developed across the roster.

But depth is a double-edged sword.

Depth means the team is strong. Depth also means the bubble is crowded.

For Alex Cook, 100 yards might not be enough to make the 53-man roster.

The numbers are cruel that way.

But he gave himself something that can't be taken away––an opportunity.

His film will be reviewed. And if the Rams don't keep him, another team might.

For Bailey, the undrafted free agent out of Louisville, it will be hard to leave him off the 53-man roster. He brings speed, athleticism, length on the edge and was dominant against the Saints.

But August dominance does not guarantee September employment.

For Lampkin, who has been cut twice and signed twice, this game was another chapter in a story written in invisible ink.

For Hamilton, the interception was a line on a resume that might get him a job in another city.

For most of these players, their dreams of regular-season action in the NFL are quickly coming to a close.

Cuts are looming, and they are near.

Phone calls will be made, tears shed, hearts broken — football lives will die.

But for one afternoon, they were all Rams.

They all fought; some made plays.

"I thought it was a really just good team effort," McVay said.

He was right. But it was also so much more. A reminder that every snap matters. Every catch, every tackle, every interception, every forced fumble matters.

Because for the men who make the most of them, those moments might be the difference between a locker and a phone call home.

A difference between a dream and a memory.

Peter Pan never had to fight for a roster spot. Peter Pan never had to run 100 yards to prove he belonged. Peter Pan's got his shadow back.

These men are still searching for theirs.
